FAST

WASHINGTON, Nov 7 : Environmental groups worldwide are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife – embracing a technology they also warn is driving a surge in electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions. The contradiction is forcing these organizations to justify their AI use in carrying out missions to combat climate change or protect natural resources. "We recognize that AI can come with environmental costs, and we need to be thoughtful about how we use it," said Ali Swanson, AI lead at the US nonprofit Conservation International. "But at a time when the climate and biodiversity crises are becoming more urgent, AI can help us move faster and make better use of the information we're collecting." The group recently started using AI to assess hotspots detected by satellites and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about potential wildfires in remote and environmentally sensitive parts of Cambodia.

Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their AI use. All said they used the technology in some form and expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers powering it. The centers, filled with servers, can require vast amounts of electricity, along with water for cooling. It's a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries balancing AI's benefits with its enormous risks. The tradeoffs likely will grab attention at the UN's COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey will call on governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge outlining principles to ensure AI is developed and deployed sustainably. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose their systems' environmental impacts. Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030, reaching a size about twice that of Jakarta, the Indonesian megalopolis. The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, estimates global data centers will consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, producing the equivalent of more than 300 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. That's double current consumption and about equal to Japan's annual electricity use. The agency also projects that global data center water consumption will increase from about 560 billion liters (147.9 billion gallons) in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters (317 billion gallons) annually by 2030. Technology giants including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet's Google have reported rising emissions linked in part to data center expansion, raising questions about their ability to meet their own long-term climate goals. Amazon told Reuters its artificial-intelligence products were among the most sustainable due to the company's purchases of low-carbon energy and its efforts to use power and water efficiently. Microsoft and Google didn't respond to requests for comment. BREAKTHROUGHS ONCE THOUGHT IMPOSSIBLE Many of the organizations that spoke to Reuters believe AI's benefits currently outweigh its costs because the technology is enabling work that was previously difficult, expensive or impossible. Kenya's Save the Elephants, a partner of the Wildlife Conservation Network, said it is using machine learning to improve population surveys and study elephant communication. Frank Pope, the group's chief executive, said an aerial survey of Kenya's largest protected area last year generated roughly 200,000 images that took nine people nine months to review manually. AI models trained on Nvidia's GeForce graphics platforms can now complete similar analyses in hours. "The results have been eye-opening," Pope said. "We found that human surveys were missing about a third of the elephants, roughly half of zebras and giraffes, and three-quarters of oryx populations." More accurate wildlife data can help secure financing for conservation, he said. "Ultimately, these tools make nature measurable and therefore investable," he said. "That's a critical transformation, if we're going to conserve biodiversity at scale." At the institute founded by the late conservation icon Jane Goodall, researchers are using AI to digitize decades of field notes about chimpanzee behavior in Tanzania's Gombe National Park. The project was once expected to take 13-15 years because the records were written by hand using the local Kiha language and scientific shorthand. Thanks to a tool developed with Amazon Web Services, the notes can now be scanned, translated and structured in minutes, slashing the time needed to about two years, said Lilian Pintea, the Jane Goodall Institute's vice president of conservation science. During her lifetime, Pintea said, Goodall supported the use of AI to advance conservation science, provided people remained firmly in control of how it was used. "AI technology should be seen as tools which are human-centered," Pintea said. LIMITING THE ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT Some organizations are experimenting with ways to limit the environmental impact of their AI use. The World Resources Institute (WRI), a research group that uses AI to accelerate its climate and environmental analyses, said it limits resource-intensive applications such as generating videos and images, while caching AI query results so identical searches don't need to be reprocessed. The US-based Nature Conservancy has adopted a similar approach. It uses AI to analyze video captured on commercial fishing vessels for information on how many fish of different species they catch. But instead of uploading huge numbers of videos to centralized data centers, it has installed AI-powered digital cameras to process information aboard the vessels, reducing energy use and data-transfer requirements, said Vienna Saccomanno, a senior scientist at the organization. "It takes a lot of engineering to make computation on the edge possible," she said. "This was worth it to reduce both our carbon footprint and deliver these sustainability insights." Greenpeace International said it, too, uses some AI tools, mainly because software platforms it relies upon include AI features. It's imposing internal guidelines emphasizing transparency, human oversight and "intentional" AI use, the group said. But it would prefer to sidestep the technology due to its environmental impacts and is pushing back hard on the data center buildout. "While other organizations are asking how to use AI responsibly, Greenpeace is asking whether it's necessary to build all these massive data centers in the first place," said Katrin Xueying Wu, a climate and energy campaigner with the organization. Other groups now see AI as vital to effective environmental activism. "It's our job to save the planet. If we can do that more effectively and efficiently with the limited resources we've got by using AI, then we have to seriously engage in that possibility," said Stuart Butchart, chief scientist at UK-based BirdLife International. "If we don't do it, then we're sort of being derelict in our duty."

(Additonal reporting by Simon Jessop in London and Kate Abnett in Brussels; Editing by Richard Valdmanis and Alexandra Zavis)

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : OpenAI has closed on new funding of $11 billion, the initial part of a round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, a source familiar with the matter said on Friday. The $11 billion raised so far represents only a portion of OpenAI's original target of up to $30 billion, while the company's valuation has come down from the $1.5 trillion level it had initially sought, two investors said. SoftBank and MGX participated in the funding, the investors said. Bloomberg News reported on the funding earlier on Friday. Sentiment toward AI companies has cooled in the last month, with some investors valuing rival Anthropic's planned IPO at about $1.5 trillion, below earlier expectations of roughly $2 trillion.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 6 : Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value were wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the AI industry. The benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq finished higher, with technology, communication services and industrials stocks driving gains. The Dow ended lower. All three indexes notched weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46 per cent, the S&P 500 rose 0.31 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.1 per cent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2 per cent after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose nearly 3 per cent, after its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel, and Micron Technology, closed up between 5 per cent and 11 per cent, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 4 per cent and nearly 9 per cent respectively after losses earlier this week. "Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management. "That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors ... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market." Texas' Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of US data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup. The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike. RIPPLE EFFECT The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe's STOXX 600 lost 1 per cent. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both slumped about 6 per cent. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff panic of April 2025. The MSCI All-World index fell 0.68 per cent while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost nearly 3 per cent. PAYROLLS BEAT FORECASTS US nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-watched pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs. An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3 per cent for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years did not materialise either, as it came in at 3.1 per cent. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.86 per cent, having dropped to its lowest level since September 9 overnight. In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52 per cent against the yen and rose 0.47 per cent against the Swiss franc. The euro was down 0.68 per cent against the dollar at $1.1142. Brent crude prices settled at $98.32, rising just 0.03 per cent, on hopes the midterms' results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war. Spot gold was flat at $4,066.28 per ounce.

Source: Reuters

FAST

CHICAGO, Nov 6 : The US Department of Agriculture will use an artificial intelligence tool it built to check data in next week's monthly crop production report, agency officials said, after a series of data missteps eroded farmers' and traders' trust in its forecasts. After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview. The tool's debut tests whether the agency can restore confidence in data that often moves markets.  "I'm very bullish on the fact that we'll be able to utilize these tools in the future to help us avoid these kinds of really, truly unfortunate errors," Hutchins said on Thursday.

Last month, the USDA corrected its September corn production and yield data. The correction raised the yield estimate by about 3 per cent in Nebraska, the third-biggest corn-producing state, and lowered it by about 2 per cent in Kansas.  The agency, long viewed as the gold standard of global agricultural market information, previously faced criticism after it made sharp upward revisions to estimates for last year's corn acreage. Over the summer, it  reported inaccurate beef export sales data. The USDA previously said it was launching a pilot project that would rely more heavily on technology to improve crop acreage and yield estimates as fewer farmers respond to its surveys.  COMPUTER FILE ERROR  Lance Honig, chair of the agricultural statistics board for USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service, told Reuters that a computer file incorrectly combined data on irrigated and non-irrigated corn acres gathered by field surveyors, causing the errors in September's data. Kansas and Nebraska were affected because they have higher percentages of irrigated fields, which often have higher yields, he said.  "This error that occurred in September is literally a very isolated occurrence that, quite frankly, with the proper validation, we should have caught," Honig said. "There was no issue with the data that was gathered at the field level." The errors angered farmers who are struggling to make money as they pay soaring prices for diesel, fertilizer and other inputs. Last month, the National Corn Growers Association, which represents 35,000 farmers, said the September errors were unacceptable and had further hurt farmers' confidence in the USDA's ability to produce accurate reports. "You just don't know what the USDA is going to do anymore," said Jim Gerlach, president of brokerage A/C Trading in Indiana, on Friday. "Their reports have become so erratic." Questions around the credibility of federal data increased after President Donald Trump's administration sharply downsized the government last year. Thousands of employees at the USDA have left, and experts have worried the cuts hobbled the agency's ability to produce accurate and timely data. Hutchins said the September errors were not related to staffing losses. The new AI tool will add to, not replace, the agency's data validation, he said.  "The tool is basically going to be used as a check to make sure that there are no anomalies that we were not able to see or identify in the normal process," Hutchins said.       This week, market analysts questioned the accuracy of another monthly USDA report on soy processing which showed a sharp divide between how many soybeans were crushed and how much soymeal was produced in Iowa.  The USDA said it was reviewing the report as part of a normal process and would make any necessary revisions next month.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : OpenAI will press ahead with its US data-center expansion plans despite a Democratic midterm sweep this week that has fueled fears of tighter scrutiny of the facilities, its Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar told CNBC in an interview on Friday. "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet customer demand," Friar said. "We are going to keep building out those relationships with communities so we can get the compute we need," she added.  One of the corporate faces of the AI boom, OpenAI has moved quickly to counter fears that a shift in congressional power could slow the industry's growth. It launched a charm offensive on Thursday to win over communities as opposition to data centers becomes a rallying point for anxieties about the technology. As part of the efforts, OpenAI said, it will no longer use non-disclosure agreements with public officials when negotiating or discussing future sites. It will also give residents access to construction plans and their potential effects.

Growing data-center opposition was a crucial issue in the midterm elections. Democratic candidates, including Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, made tighter scrutiny of the facilities a central campaign pledge. The Lone Star State is one of the fastest-growing data-center regions in the world. Fears the Democratic sweep may slow construction of the facilities critical to the AI boom wiped about $2.5 trillion off the US stock market on Thursday, as investors weighed the fallout for the chip, cloud and networking industries that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the spending frenzy. Still, there are signs that tech giants remain committed to data-center expansion plans despite the growing backlash. Alphabet-owned Google said on Thursday it would invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming. Meanwhile, Bloomberg News reported that ByteDance is considering expanding a data center project in northeastern Brazil, a move that would strengthen its standing as Latin America's leading builder of computing facilities. OPENAI'S FUNDRAISING PLANS Friar also told CNBC that OpenAI was raising fresh capital, pushing back against suggestions the ChatGPT maker had scaled back its fundraising ambitions amid the sharp AI stocks selloff. The company is seeking fresh capital after its business grew 70 per cent quarter over quarter in the third quarter, with enterprise demand doubling over the same period, she said. "It (the growth) is saying people are actually using AI and getting value from it," Friar said. The fundraising comes as the market turmoil is raising questions about OpenAI rival Anthropic's widely awaited listing. Reuters reported on Thursday that prospective investors in Anthropic's IPO are questioning whether the AI startup can begin its roadshow next week and stay on track for a November listing. Investors are pushing for a more attractive valuation to commit to the offering, with some viewing the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations, four people familiar with investor discussions told Reuters.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle as part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Shares of Oracle and Microsoft were flat in afternoon trading. Both stocks had come under pressure this week after a Democratic midterm election sweep in the US raised worries about tighter scrutiny that could threaten the AI industry's breakneck expansion. Microsoft had been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle in recent months after declining to renew the contract, according to the Bloomberg report. The rented computing capacity became less valuable over time as it no longer met Microsoft's evolving needs, the report added, noting that the Oracle hardware used an older generation of Nvidia chips.

WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Friday the central bank expects underlying inflation to stay around its 2 per cent target but recognizes there are "some upside risks". The rise in prices of energy-related products was beginning to hit consumer inflation with price growth seen accelerating further into early next year, Ueda said. "We are in an equilibrium with wages growing at a level consistent with 2 per cent inflation," Ueda said at a seminar hosted by the International Monetary Fund. But the BOJ's 2 per cent inflation target has yet to become a social norm in Japan, Ueda said, adding that the central bank's goal now was to anchor underlying inflation around its target.

He also said the BOJ was looking at the actions of other central banks "very, very carefully," as they affect asset prices including foreign exchange rates and interest rates. "What they do reveals important information about what they think about their economies, which will impact our economy. So we look at their behavior and actions very carefully," he said on the policy measures of other central banks. On unconventional monetary policy tools, Ueda said they have had some positive effects when the BOJ deployed them, but added they have not been perfect substitutes for cutting interest rates from positive territory. The BOJ may be obliged to deploy unconventional policy tools again depending on the severity of the economic shock that may hit Japan, Ueda said. "I guess the important thing would be to keep inflation or underlying inflation at around 2 per cent as much as possible. But if we need to deploy these tools again, we should think about ways to minimize negative effects, including possibly the effect on the functioning of the market," he said. Asked about discussions sparked by new Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh about excessive communication, Ueda said central banks needed a good balance between the need to communicate policy goals and the risk of creating a moral hazard on the part of the market. "There has to be a good balance between these considerations," he said, adding that in Japan's case, it had been using underlying inflation as a key variable in guiding policy. Having reached 2 per cent underlying inflation, its goal now was to keep it there, he said. AI, CYBER CHALLENGES Ueda commented briefly on the promise and risks of artificial intelligence, saying rapid advancements in AI had provided a positive demand shock for the Japanese economy, but supply side factors would also need to be studied. Unlike some other countries, Japan could do well with AI replacing labor given its significant labor shortages, he said. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, noting recent market weakness around AI stocks, said central bankers around the world would need to consider any slowdown in AI-driven growth as they assess steps in their fight against inflation. Georgieva said concerns about dependence on the AI investment boom and high valuations were impacting markets around the world. "Things are going up and down, and this is likely to continue," she told an audience of hundreds at the IMF headquarters in Washington who came to hear Ueda, adding that the volatility would complicate the job of central banks at a time when risks to price stability had been growing. Ueda said he also worried about cyber risks in terms of financial stability, adding that some small banks and small firms had not done enough to guard against such risks.

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Nov 6 : A rout in technology stocks as confidence in the AI trade falters could test the resilience of global financial markets from New York to Taipei. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 rose nearly 2 per cent on Friday, clawing back some of Thursday's more than 6 per cent plunge - but traders remain on edge. Policymakers have long warned of the risks from an AI boom unraveling. Investors and regulators are keeping a close watch on market stress indicators, with some flashing amber, although not yet red. Here's a look at how key measures are faring:

FEAR IS UP Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX index of US stock market volatility, rose to over 28 on Thursday, its highest since late March. It was holding close to that level on Friday. The increase is relatively contained compared to the post-April 2025 "Liberation Day" market jump and the August 2024 market selloff. Still, the VIX has surged more than 40 per cent this week. The European equivalent hit its highest level since May on Friday. "It's still early days," said Idanna Appio, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments. "My concern would be if we see more spikes in volatility, more stress, real issues with the ability to access markets. Those will be the things that...I'll be watching." PROTECTION FROM TECH TREMORS Perhaps the biggest harbinger of potential trouble in the AI space is a surge in insurance protection against a debt default. The cost of insuring debt issued by neocloud firm CoreWeave has spiked into distressed territory, with five-year credit default swap (CDS) spreads surging past 1,000 basis points to record highs. It has become a barometer of investor anxiety over AI. Spreads on credit default swaps for SpaceX and Intel have also jumped this week. The premium investors demand to hold US high yield corporate credit, known as junk bonds, has risen to its highest since the Liberation Day ructions as traders cool on riskier assets. In the riskiest parts of the market, for companies rated CCC or lower, that premium is trading at around its highest since 2020, according to ICE BofA indices. INVESTORS SEEK SAFETY A flight to safe havens is a clear sign of increased market angst, although daily moves are also relatively modest. US 10-year Treasury yields have fallen 50 bps from peaks above 5 per cent hit last month on concerns about high debt, rising inflation and competition for capital as tech firms ramped up bond sales. Currency markets were relatively muted, but there were some signs of investors seeking the US dollar, which was up 0.6 per cent as of 1500 GMT on Friday. Three-month euro cross-currency basis swaps, or the relative premium for swapping foreign currencies into dollars, briefly touched -8 bps on Thursday, the lowest since late 2023, signaling increased demand for dollar funding. It had recovered slightly on Friday to around -6 bps. BofA's Flow Show report on Friday said cash funds saw a $140 billion inflow in the week to Wednesday, the seventh biggest on record. BONDS BEHAVE Bond markets are so far showing no signs of the sort of stress they came under during the COVID-19 pandemic or around the Liberation Day tariffs. The closely watched MOVE index, which tracks volatility in the US Treasury market, hit a six-month high in October but has since slipped back. Other bond-market measures such as US swap spreads, which can indicate funding and liquidity stress, have also remained calm.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 6 : Firefly Aerospace will supply core engines for a new rocket under development by satellite communications firm AST SpaceMobile in a $1.3 billion deal, underscoring a push among satellite companies to secure access to space. The engine deal, announced on Friday, is a key part of new plans by AST SpaceMobile to develop its own rocket named Blacklift as it races to deploy a satellite constellation for global cellular broadband service and wean itself off a reliance on third-party rockets like SpaceX's Falcon 9. Firefly will build and supply 27 of its new Miranda engines and 9 in-space Vira engines for the first three Blacklift rockets, per the agreement, which also grants a license to AST to eventually manufacture the engines itself. Shares of Firefly were up about 18 per cent following the announcement of the deal, while AST SpaceMobile's stock was up about 1 per cent.

AST said it is targeting late 2028 for the debut launch of Blacklift, an ambitious development timeline. The company said the rocket is "designed for reusability" and can loft up to five of its BlueBird satellites per launch. Satellite companies have faced difficulty booking rides to space in the past year as major rocket launch companies — like Elon Musk's SpaceX and, in future, Rocket Lab — increasingly dedicate their mission manifests to their own satellite constellation deployments. AST said it still plans to use external rockets and has over 100 launch agreements in place as it targets a total deployment of 248 satellites to complete its global broadband network, which is designed to beam service directly to mobile phones. Roughly a dozen of its BlueBird satellites have launched since 2024 on rockets from SpaceX, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin and the Indian Space Research Organisation. In April, an issue with Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket doomed a BlueBird satellite to a lower-than-planned region of space that led to its deorbital demise days later. US ROCKET RAMP-UP For Firefly, the AST agreement brings in needed cash to speed up production and testing with its Alpha rocket and a next-generation rocket in development, Eclipse, whose first launch is planned for sometime in 2027. Firefly CEO Jason Kim said the deal, valued at more than $1.3 billion, "supercharges Firefly's production system — more test bays at our Rocket Ranch, long-lead materials bought ahead, and a bigger team of engineers and technicians." Rocket Ranch is the company's rocket manufacturing and testing hub in Briggs, Texas, about 20 miles (32 km) from its headquarters outside Austin. The Miranda engine is also the heart of Firefly's Eclipse. The company's Alpha rocket uses a different engine called Reaver. Firefly in 2021 signed a similar deal for its Reaver rocket engine with launch startup Astra Space that included engine deliveries and an intellectual property agreement allowing Astra to produce Reavers in-house, with some competitive restrictions on how Astra could use the engine for its own rockets. It was not immediately clear what, if any, restrictions were included in Firefly's AST agreement, but the company in a statement described it as a "Non-Competitive Deal: AST SpaceMobile will launch their own satellites, and Firefly will continue to serve the broader government and commercial launch market." The deal is the latest display of US rocket production ramp-ups as the space industry confronts global scarcity in launch options, with SpaceX's dominant Falcon 9 nearing retirement in the coming years while its next-generation Starship rocket foments a broader industry pivot toward large, vertically integrated launch systems. Blue Origin on Thursday revealed a new rocket engine named Northstar and an expansion to its New Glenn rocket that adds a third rocket stage, optimizing the vehicle to carry heavier payloads to more precise locations in space.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : Fox Corp on Friday completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, a major bet that the streaming platform will bolster the broadcaster's advertising business and expand the online reach of its sports and news programming. Announced in June, the cash-and-stock deal gives Fox access to the more than 100 million households using Roku's platform, potentially helping the cable TV-reliant media company build a larger digital audience and better target ads.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : Charter Communications said on Friday it would cut $2 billion in annualized operating costs over the next 18 months as part of an overhaul of its operating model aimed at reviving growth in a competitive cable and broadband market.  Shares of the company fell 2.7 per cent in morning trading. They have fallen 39.7 per cent so far this year through Thursday's close. Charter said it would revamp how it markets and sells its core internet service and lean more on its mobile and video products to add customers and improve retention. Charter has "not generated the customer growth and performance we expect," CEO Chris Winfrey said on a post-earnings call.

The cost cuts are separate from more than $1 billion in anticipated synergies from Charter's acquisition of Cox Communications, which closed on August 19. The $34.5 billion deal, including debt, combined two of the largest US cable and broadband operators as Netflix, Disney+, Verizon and T-Mobile intensify competition for customers. Charter lost 233,000 internet customers in the third quarter on a pro forma basis, versus a loss of 171,000 a year earlier, while video customers fell by 77,000, compared with a decline of 121,000. "Charter’s mounting broadband losses are alarming and underscore the scale of the challenge," said Paolo Pescatore, founder of PP Foresight. The $2 billion cost-cutting program is necessary, but "it cannot simply cut its way back to growth," he added. Charter on Friday reported third-quarter revenue of $14.9 billion, below analysts' average estimate of $15.03 billion, according to LSEG data.  It posted a net loss of $20.50 per share, versus income of $8.50 last year, driven mainly by a $6.3 billion franchise impairment charge. The company had total debt of $108.6 billion at the end of September, against cash of $573 million. Separately, Reuters reported on Tuesday India's Jio Platforms has held talks with Charter and Comcast about licensing its wireless broadband technology for potential stakes.

Source: Reuters
